cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK XXIV
The second Nekyia;\nLaertes and the trees; the peace of Ithaca.
And Hermes of Cyllene was calling out the souls\nof the suitor-men. He held in his hands the rod,
beautiful, golden, with which he charms men's eyes
to sleep, whose eyes he wills,\nand wakes others from their slumber;
with this he set them moving and led them,\nand they followed, squeaking.
As when bats in the corner of a wondrous\ncave flit squeaking, when one drops off
the chain of them clinging to the rock and to each other:
so these went with him, squeaking; and Hermes\nthe kindly led them down along the dank ways.
Past the streams of Ocean they went, past the White Rock,
past the gates of the Sun and the country of dreams,\nand soon they came to the meadow of asphodel,
where the souls have their dwelling —\nthe phantoms of the worn-out dead.
There they found the soul of Achilles, Peleus' son,\nand of Patroclus, and of blameless Antilochus,
and of Ajax, who was first in beauty and in build of\nall the Danaans after the blameless son of Peleus.
These were gathered around Achilles; and close\nto them came the soul of Agamemnon, Atreus' son,
grieving; and around him others\nwere gathered — all who died
beside him in Aegisthus' house, and met their fate.
And the soul of Peleus' son spoke to him first:
"Son of Atreus, we used to say that you, of all the\nhero-men, were dear to Zeus who delights in thunder
all your days — because you were lord over many strong men
in the land of the Trojans, where we Achaeans suffered.
And yet it was to you that ruinous doom would\ncome so early — the doom no man born escapes.
If only, in the fullness of the honor you were lord of,
you had met your death and fate\nin the land of the Trojans:
then all the Achaeans together would have made your tomb,
and you would have won great fame for your son hereafter.
As it was, your portion was to be\ncaught by the most pitiful of deaths."
Then the soul of Atreus' son answered him:
"Blessed son of Peleus, Achilles like the gods,\nwho died at Troy, far from Argos — and around you the others
fell, the best of the sons of Trojans and Achaeans,
fighting over your body; and you in the swirl of the dust
lay great in your greatness, your horsemanship forgotten.
And we fought the whole day through, and would never
have ceased from the fighting,\nhad Zeus not stopped us with a storm.
And when we had carried you\nout of the battle to the ships,
we laid you on a bier, and cleansed your beautiful body
with warm water and with oil; and over you the\nDanaans shed many hot tears, and cut their hair.
And out of the sea your mother came,\nwith the deathless sea-women,
when she heard the news; and a cry went up over the deep,
unearthly — and trembling took hold of all the Achaeans.
They would have sprung up then\nand fled to the hollow ships,
had not a man held them back, one deep in old wisdom:
Nestor, whose counsel had shown truest long before.
With good will toward them he spoke out and said:
'Hold, Argives! Do not run, young men of the Achaeans!
It is his mother coming out of the sea, with the\ndeathless sea-women, to look on the face of her dead son.'
So he spoke, and the great-hearted\nAchaeans checked their flight.
And around you stood the daughters\nof the old man of the sea,
mourning piteously; and they wrapped\nyou in imperishable clothing.
And the Muses, all nine, answering voice to lovely voice,\nsang the dirge. Not one Argive could you have seen
unweeping then, so keen was the clear Muse's song.
Seventeen days together, nights and days alike,\nwe mourned you — deathless gods and mortal men;
on the eighteenth we gave you to the fire, and around you
slaughtered fat sheep in plenty and spiral-horned cattle.
You burned in the clothing of the gods, in oil in\nplenty and in sweet honey; and many Achaean heroes
moved in armor around your burning pyre,\nmen on foot and horsemen, and a great roar went up.
And when the flame of Hephaestus had made an end of you,\nat dawn we gathered your white bones, Achilles,
into unmixed wine and oil. Your mother gave\na golden two-eared jar — a gift of Dionysus,
she said, and the work of famous Hephaestus.
In that lie your white bones, shining Achilles,\nmingled with the bones of dead Patroclus, Menoetius' son,
and apart lie Antilochus', whom you honored beyond\nall your other companions after Patroclus died.
And over them all we heaped a great and blameless\ntomb — we, the sacred army of Argive spearmen —
on a jutting headland over the broad Hellespont,\nso it might be seen far off, from the open sea,
by men now living and by men to come.
And your mother asked the gods for prizes of great beauty
and set them in the middle of the field,\nfor the best of the Achaeans.
You have stood by now at the funeral games of many\nheroes — when a king has died, and the young men
belt themselves and make ready for the prizes —\nbut had you seen those, your heart would have wondered most:
what beautiful prizes the goddess set out in your honor,
silver-footed Thetis. For you were most dear to the gods.
So not even in death did you lose your name: forever,\namong all mankind, your fame will be noble, Achilles.
But I? What joy of it had I,\nwhen I had wound the war to its end?
On my homecoming Zeus devised a wretched death for\nme at the hands of Aegisthus and my accursed wife."
So they spoke to one another of such things.
And the guide came near them, the slayer of Argus,\nleading down the souls of the suitors Odysseus broke;
and the two, amazed,\nwent straight toward them at the sight.
And the soul of Agamemnon, Atreus' son,\nknew the dear son of Melaneus, far-famed Amphimedon:
for he had been his guest-friend, with his home in Ithaca.
The soul of Atreus' son spoke to him first:
"Amphimedon, what has happened to you,\nthat you plunge under the dark earth,
all of you picked men, all of an age? A man choosing\nthe best in a city could not have chosen better.
Did Poseidon break you in your ships,\nraising cruel winds and long waves?
Or did enemies on land destroy you while you were\ncutting out their cattle and fine flocks of sheep,
or as they fought for their city and their women?
Answer what I ask: I declare myself your guest-friend.
Do you not remember when I came to your house there,\nwith godlike Menelaus, to urge Odysseus
to follow with us to Ilium on the well-benched ships?
A whole month it took us to cross all that wide sea,\nand hard work to win over Odysseus, sacker of cities."
Then the soul of Amphimedon answered him:
"Most glorious son of Atreus, Agamemnon lord of men,\nI remember all of it, Zeus-nurtured, as you tell it;
and I will recount to you everything, fully and truly —
the evil end of our death, how it was brought to pass.
We were courting the wife of Odysseus —\nof the man so long away.
She neither refused the marriage she\nloathed, nor would she make an end,
plotting for us death and the black doom;\nno — here is another trick her heart devised:
she set up a great loom in the halls and wove at it,
fine-threaded, beyond all measure wide,\nand told us straightway:
'Young men, my suitors — since noble Odysseus is dead,\nwait, though you burn for my wedding, till I finish
this cloth — let my spinning not be wasted on the wind —\na shroud for the hero Laertes, against the day
the ruinous doom of death that lays men low will take him:
let no Achaean woman in the land hold it against me
that a man who won so much should\nlie without his winding-sheet.'
So she spoke, and our proud hearts were persuaded.
Then every day she wove at the great loom,\nand every night she unwove it by torchlight.
Three years her trick escaped us,\nand she kept the Achaeans persuaded;
but when the fourth year came, as the seasons rolled on,
the months waning away, the long tale of days accomplished,\nthen one of her women, who knew it all, told us,
and we caught her unweaving the shining web.
So she finished it — against her will, under force.
And when she had shown us the robe — the great web woven\nand washed — and it shone like the sun or the moon,
just then some evil god brought Odysseus from somewhere
to the border of the land,\nwhere the swineherd had his house.
There came also the dear son of godlike Odysseus,\nback in his black ship out of sandy Pylos;
and the two of them plotted an evil death for the\nsuitors and came to the famous town — Odysseus
later; it was Telemachus who led the way before him.
The swineherd brought the master, in bad clothes on his body,\nin the likeness of a beggar, wretched and old,
leaning on a stick, with miserable clothing on his body;
and not one of us could know him for the man he was,
breaking on us suddenly like that —\nnot even the older men —
no: we went at him with ugly words,\nand with things thrown.
And he for a while endured it in his own halls,\npelted and taunted, with an enduring heart;
but when the mind of Zeus who bears the aegis roused him,\nwith Telemachus he lifted the beautiful armor away
and stowed it in the storeroom and shot the bolts,\nand then — his cunning at work — he ordered his wife
to set before the suitors the bow and the gray iron,
the contest for us star-crossed men,\nand the beginning of the slaughter.
And not one of us could stretch the string of\nthat strong bow: we fell far, far short of it.
But when the great bow came into Odysseus' hands,\nthen all of us together shouted out threats
not to give him the bow, however much he pleaded;\nonly Telemachus urged him on and commanded it.
And he took it in his hand, much-enduring noble Odysseus,
and strung the bow with ease, and shot through the iron,
and went and stood on the threshold,\nand poured out the swift arrows,
glaring terribly — and he shot Antinous the king.
And then he sent his groaning shafts into the others,\naiming straight ahead; and they fell in heaps.
It was plain some god was their helper in the fight:
for storming down the hall in their fury they\nkilled left and right, and hideous groaning rose
as heads were smashed, and the\nwhole floor smoked with blood.
So we perished, Agamemnon — and even now our\nbodies lie uncared-for in the halls of Odysseus:
for the friends in each man's house do not yet know —\nthe ones who would wash the black gore from our wounds
and lay us out with wailing:\nfor that is the portion of the dead."
Then the soul of Atreus' son answered him:
"Blessed son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many devices —\ntruly you won a wife of great excellence!
How sound the mind of blameless Penelope,\nIcarius' daughter! How faithfully she kept the memory
of Odysseus, her wedded husband!\nAnd so the fame of her excellence
will never perish; and the deathless ones will make
a song for those on earth, a song of\ngrace, for steady-hearted Penelope —
not like the daughter of Tyndareus, who plotted evil,\nwho killed her wedded husband: a song of loathing
she will be among mankind; and she brings hard fame
on all women — on womankind, even on those who do right."
So the two of them spoke to one another of such things,
standing in the house of Hades,\nunder the hidden places of the earth.
And the others — when they had gone\ndown from the city, they soon reached
the beautiful well-worked farm\nof Laertes, which Laertes himself
had won long ago, when his labors for it were many.
There was his house, and running all around it the\nsheds where the bound slaves ate, and sat, and slept —
the ones whose labor did his will.
And in the house was an old Sicilian woman, who cared
for the old man devotedly,\nout on the farm far from the town.
And there Odysseus spoke to the slaves and to his son:
"You now — go inside the well-built house,\nand slaughter for dinner, right away, the best of the pigs;
and I will make a trial of my father — whether he\nwill know me, whether his eyes will make me out,
or fail to know a son so long away."
So speaking he handed the slaves his weapons of war.
They went quickly on into the house; and Odysseus\nmoved up toward the fruited orchard, testing.
And going down into the great garden he found no Dolius,
none of the slaves, none of the sons: they had gone\noff gathering fieldstones for the orchard wall,
and the old man had led them the way.
So he found his father alone in the well-worked orchard,\nspading round a young tree — in a filthy tunic,
patched, disgraceful; round his shins he had bound\nstitched leggings of oxhide, to fend off the scratches,
and gloves on his hands because of the thorns;\nand on his head he wore a goatskin cap — feeding his sorrow.
And when much-enduring noble Odysseus saw him —\nbroken with old age, the great grief packed inside him —
he stopped beneath a towering pear tree, and wept.
Then he weighed it in his mind and in his heart:
to kiss his father, and hold him,\nand tell him everything —
how he had come, how he had reached his fathers' land —
or question him first, and test him through and through.
And as he weighed it, this seemed to him the better way:
to try him first with words that bite.
With this in mind, noble Odysseus went straight up to him.
He was holding his head down, spading round his tree,\nand standing beside him his shining son spoke to him:
"Old man — no lack of skill in you at\ntending an orchard! Not one thing —
no plant, no fig tree, no vine, no olive, no pear tree,\nno vegetable bed — goes untended in this garden.
But another thing I will say —\nand do not take anger into your heart:
you — you are not well kept. Hard old age is on you,
and with it you are shabby with\ngrime, and clothed in disgrace.
It cannot be for idleness that your master neglects you;
and there is nothing of the slave to be seen in you,
in your face or your stature: you look like a kingly man.
You look like one who, after his bath and his dinner,
should sleep on softness:\nfor that is the right of the old.
But come, tell me this, and tell it to me truly:
Whose slave are you? Whose orchard do you tend?
And tell me this too, honestly, so that I may know it:
is this land we have come to truly Ithaca,\nas that man told me who met me on the road just now —
not too well furnished in the wits: he had not the\npatience to tell me everything or hear out my question
about a guest-friend of mine — whether he lives still,\nor is dead by now, and down in the house of Hades.
For I will tell you this; mark it and hear me:
I once played host, in my own dear country, to a man\nwho came to our place; and never has another mortal
of all the far-come strangers\nbeen more welcome in my house.
He declared his stock was out of Ithaca;\nhe said his father was Laertes, Arceisius' son.
So I brought him to the house and gave him welcome,\nwarm and openhanded — the house had plenty in it —
and I gave him gifts of friendship, such as fitted:
seven talents of well-worked gold I gave him,\na mixing-bowl all silver, worked with flowers,
twelve single cloaks, as many coverlets,\nas many beautiful mantles, tunics with them,
and besides all this, four women skilled in blameless
handwork, good-looking ones —\nhis own choice, whichever he would."
And his father answered him, weeping:
"Stranger, you have come indeed to the land you ask for —\nbut violent men hold it now, men lost to decency.
The gifts you showered on him —\nthe countless gifts — were wasted.
If you had found him alive in the land of Ithaca,\nhe would have sent you off well matched in gifts,
well hosted too: that is the law,\nfor whoever begins the kindness.
But come, tell me this, and tell it to me truly:
how many years is it since you hosted him — that guest\nof yours, that luckless man — my son, if he ever was:
my ill-starred son? Whom, far from\nhis friends and his fathers' land,
either the fish have eaten in the sea, or on dry ground
he has become the spoil of\nbeasts and birds; and his mother
never shrouded and mourned him,\nnor his father — we who bore him;
nor did his richly dowered wife, steady-hearted Penelope,
keen over her own husband on the bier, as was fitting,
or close his eyes: and that is the portion of the dead.
And tell me this too, honestly, so that I may know it:
What man are you, and from where?\nWhere are your city and your parents?
And where is the fast ship standing that brought you here
with your godlike companions? Or did you come a passenger
on another's ship, which set you down and went on?"
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Then I will tell you everything exactly.
I am from Alybas, where I have my famous house:
son of Apheidas, the son of lord Polypemon;\nmy own name is Eperitus. But a god
drove me wandering here from Sicania, against my will,
and my ship stands off the fields, away from the town.
As for Odysseus — this is now the fifth year\nsince he went from there, and left my country —
the ill-starred man! And yet the\nbirds were good when he set out:
on the right; and I rejoiced in them as I sent him off,
And the heart in both of us hoped
we would meet again as guest-friends,\nand give each other shining gifts."
So he spoke; and a black cloud\nof grief closed over the old man:
with both hands he scooped up the scorched gray dust
and poured it down over his white head,\nsobbing thick and fast.
And the heart of Odysseus was shaken;\nup through his nostrils
shot the sharp sting of tears —\nhis father before his eyes.
He sprang to him, and caught\nhim in his arms, and kissed him:
"Father — I am he. I myself, the man you ask for,\ncome home in the twentieth year to my fathers' land.
Stop now — no more weeping, no more tears and mourning.
For I tell you this — and the need to hurry is very great:
I have killed the suitors in our own halls;
I have punished their heart-stinging\noutrage and their evil deeds."
Then Laertes answered him and said:
"If you are truly Odysseus — my son — come home,\ntell me some sign, some plain one, so I can believe."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"First — this scar: see it with your own eyes —\nwhere the boar dealt me its white tusk, on Parnassus,
the time I went there. It was you\nwho sent me — you and my honored
mother — to Autolycus, her dear father, to collect
the gifts he promised me,\nand nodded to, when he came here.
And then — come — let me tell you\nthe trees in the well-worked orchard
you gave me once. I was begging you for each of them,
a little boy, trailing you through the garden. We wound
among these very trees, and you named them one by one:
you gave me thirteen pear trees, and ten apple trees,\nand forty fig trees; and you named fifty rows of vines
as mine to come, each one ripening in its own turn —\nclusters of every kind hanging along them —
whenever the seasons of Zeus\ncame down and weighed them low."
So he spoke; and the old man's knees went\nslack where he stood, and his dear heart,
as he recognized the tokens Odysseus described so surely.
He threw his arms around his dear son — and fainting
he was caught against him by much-enduring noble Odysseus.
And when he had got his breath,\nand the spirit gathered back into his heart,
once more he found his words, and answered:
"Father Zeus — you gods are still there on high Olympus,
if truly the suitors have paid for their reckless outrage!
But now the terror in my heart is this: that soon\nthe men of Ithaca will all come here against us,
and send out messengers everywhere,\nto every Cephallenian town."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Courage. Do not let that\ntrouble the heart in your breast.
Come — let us go to the house\nthat stands here by the orchard:
I sent Telemachus ahead there, with the cowherd and the\nswineherd, to make the meal as quickly as they can."
So the two of them talked,\nand made their way to the beautiful house.
And when they came to the well-settled house,\nthey found Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd
carving meat in plenty and mixing the sparkling wine.
Meanwhile the great-hearted Laertes, in his own house,
was bathed by the Sicilian serving-woman,\nand rubbed with oil,
and she threw a beautiful cloak around him; and Athena
came and stood close by,\nand filled out the limbs of the shepherd
of the people: taller than before\nshe made him, and broader to the eye.
Out of the bath he came; and his dear son wondered at him,\nseeing him face to face like the deathless gods,
and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
"Father — surely one of the gods who are forever has\nmade you finer to look at, in beauty and in stature!"
Then Laertes the clear-headed answered him:
"If only — father Zeus, Athena, Apollo! —\nsuch a man as I was when I took Nericus, the strong-built
citadel on the mainland cape,\nlording it over the Cephallenians —
such a man, in armor, I had stood beside you yesterday\nin our own house, and beaten at the suitor-men:
then I would have unstrung the knees of many of them
there in the halls — and the heart\nin you would have been glad!"
So they spoke to one another of such things.
And when the others had finished\ntheir work and made the meal,
they sat down in order on the benches and the chairs,
and were just putting their\nhands to the food, when up came
the old man Dolius, and with him the old man's sons,
tired out from their field-work: their mother had gone out
and called them — the old Sicilian woman, who raised them
and tended the old man devotedly,\nnow that age had hold of him.
And when they saw Odysseus, and their hearts took it in,\nthey stopped in the hall, astounded. But Odysseus
fastened on them with gentle words and said:
"Old man — sit down to dinner,\nand all of you, forget your wonder.
We have been waiting in the hall a long while, eager
to put our hands to the bread,\nexpecting you every minute."
So he spoke; and Dolius came straight at him, both arms
spread wide; and he caught Odysseus'\nhand and kissed it at the wrist,
and lifting his voice he spoke winged words:
"Dear master — since you have\ncome home to us who longed for you
and had given up believing,\nand the gods themselves have brought you:
health, and all joy to you,\nand may the gods give you happiness!
But tell me this thing truly, so that I may know it:
does watchful-minded Penelope know already that\nyou are home — or shall we send a messenger?"
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Old man, she knows already.\nWhy should you be busied with that?"
So he spoke; and Dolius sat\nback down on the polished stool.
And in the same way the sons of\nDolius, around famous Odysseus,
pressed his hands and welcomed him with words,\nand sat down in order beside Dolius their father.
So they were busy with dinner in the house.
But Rumor the messenger went\ndarting through the city everywhere,
crying the hateful death and doom of the suitors.
And the people heard it all at once, and gathered
from every side, with groans and wailing,\nbefore the house of Odysseus.
Each family carried its dead out\nof the house, and buried them;
and the dead of the other cities they sent home,\nlaying each man aboard the fishermen's fast ships;
and they went in a body to the\nassembly-place, grieving at heart.
And when they were assembled, all gathered together,\nEupeithes rose among them and spoke:
for a grief there was no forgetting lay upon his heart —
for his son, Antinous, the first man noble Odysseus killed;\nweeping for him he rose and spoke among them:
"Friends — a monstrous work this man\nhas wrought against the Achaeans!
Some he led off in the ships — many men, and brave ones —\nand he lost the hollow ships, and lost the people;
and some he has killed on his return —\nfar the best of the Cephallenians.
Come then — before he can get away quickly to Pylos,\nor to shining Elis, where the Epeians hold power —
let us move! Or we hang our heads in shame forever after.
This is a disgrace even for men unborn to hear of,\nif we do not take vengeance on the murderers of our sons
and our brothers. For me —\nthere would be no sweetness left
in living: I would rather die at\nonce and be among the perished.
Move — before they get across the water and away from us!"
So he spoke, weeping; and pity\ntook hold of all the Achaeans.
But now Medon came up to them, and the godlike singer,
out of the halls of Odysseus, for sleep had let them go;
they stood in the middle of them;\nand amazement took every man.
And Medon, whose mind knew wisdom, spoke among them:
"Hear me now, men of Ithaca. Not without the will of\nthe deathless gods did Odysseus devise these things.
I myself saw a deathless god, who stood close beside\nOdysseus, and looked in all things like Mentor;
and this deathless god now showed in front of Odysseus,\nheartening him — and now he stormed the hall,
stampeding the suitors; and they fell in heaps."
So he spoke; and the pale terror took hold of them all.
And the old hero Halitherses spoke among them,\nMastor's son — for he alone saw before and behind:
with good will toward them he spoke out and said:
"Hear me now, men of Ithaca, hear what I say.
By your own fault, friends,\nthese things have come to pass:
you would not listen to me,\nnor to Mentor, shepherd of the people,
and make your sons leave off their reckless folly —
your sons who did a monstrous\nwork in their wicked blindness,
shearing away the goods and dishonoring the wife
of a man of the first rank,\nsaying he would come home no more.
So now — let it rest here. Do as I say:
do not march. Some of us may draw\nthe evil down on his own head."
So he spoke; and more than half leapt up with a great\nbattle-shout — but the rest stayed there in a body:
for the word did not please them\nin their hearts; it was Eupeithes
they followed; and they rushed at once for their weapons.
And when they had cased their\nflesh in the flashing bronze,
they gathered in a body before the wide-spaced town;\nand Eupeithes led them, in his folly:
he was sure he would avenge the\nkilling of his son — and he was never
to come back again: he was to meet his own fate there.
And now Athena spoke to Zeus, the son of Cronos:
"Father of us all, son of Cronos, highest of the mighty,
answer me when I ask: what is your mind hiding now within?
Will you push on with evil war and the terrible\nbattle-din, or set the two sides now in friendship?"
Then Zeus who gathers the clouds answered her:
"My child, why do you ask me? Why question me on this?
Was it not you who framed this plan yourself —\nthat Odysseus should come home and pay those men in full?
Do as you will. But I will tell you what is fitting.
Now that noble Odysseus has paid the suitors out,\nlet them cut faithful oaths — he to be king all his days —
and let us, for our part, set a forgetting of the killing\nof sons and of brothers. Let them love one another
as before; and let wealth and peace be there in plenty."
So speaking he stirred Athena — eager long before —\nand down she went darting from the peaks of Olympus.
Now when they had put from them\nthe desire for honey-hearted food,
much-enduring noble Odysseus began among them:
"Someone go out and look —\nin case they are close, and coming."
So he spoke; and a son of Dolius went out, as he ordered,
and stood on the threshold,\nand saw them — all of them — near,
and quickly he spoke winged words to Odysseus:
"Here they are — close! Quick — to arms!"
Up they sprang and got into their armor —\nthe four around Odysseus, and the six sons of Dolius;
and with them Laertes and Dolius got\ninto armor too, gray though they were.
And when they had cased their\nflesh in the flashing bronze,
they opened the doors and went out; and Odysseus led.
And near them came the daughter of Zeus,\nAthena, likened to Mentor in body and in voice;
and much-enduring noble Odysseus\nwas glad at the sight of her,
and quickly he spoke to Telemachus his dear son:
"Telemachus — now you will learn\nit for yourself, standing where
men fight it out, and the best are sorted from the rest:
shame nothing of your fathers' line.\nIn strength and manhood
we have excelled from of old across the whole earth."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"You will see me, if you care to look,\ndear father, in this temper
shaming nothing of your line — as you have said."
So he spoke; and Laertes exulted, and cried out:
"What a day this is for me, dear gods! Great is my joy:
my son and my son's son are striving over excellence!"
And gray-eyed Athena came and stood by him and said:
"Son of Arceisius — far the dearest of all my companions —
pray to the gray-eyed girl, and to Zeus her father,\nthen swing the long-shadowed spear up, and let it fly."
So spoke Pallas Athena,\nand breathed great strength into him;
and he prayed then to the daughter of great Zeus,\nand swung the long-shadowed spear up, and let it fly,
and struck Eupeithes through the bronze-cheeked helmet:
the helmet did not stop the spear;\nthe point drove through,
and he fell with a crash,\nand his armor clattered upon him.
And Odysseus and his shining son fell on the front-fighters,\nhacking with swords and double-pointed spears;
and they would have destroyed them all,\ncut them off from homecoming,
had not Athena, daughter of Zeus who bears the aegis,\ncried out with her voice, and checked the whole array:
"Hold back, men of Ithaca, from grinding war —\nseparate now, quickly, and without blood!"
So spoke Athena; and the pale terror seized them:
out of their frightened hands the weapons flew,\nand all fell on the ground at the goddess's cry,
and they turned toward the city, aching to live.
And terribly then cried out much-enduring noble Odysseus,
and gathering himself he swooped like a high-flown eagle.
But then the son of Cronos let fly his smoking bolt,
and it fell in front of the gray-eyed one,\nthe great Father's daughter.
And then gray-eyed Athena said to Odysseus:
"Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many\ndevices, hold! Stop the strife of leveling war —
for fear the son of Cronos be angered\nwith you: Zeus of the wide voice."
So spoke Athena. He obeyed — and his heart was glad.
And a sworn peace between the\ntwo sides, for all days to come,
was set by Pallas Athena, daughter of Zeus who bears\nthe aegis, likened to Mentor in body and in voice.
